1 Introduction

Welcome to the second workshop. We will continue working with the Lending Club data. In this workshop we will take the perspective of an investor to the lending club. Our goal is to select a subset of the most promising loans to invest in. We will do so using the method of logistic regression. Feel free to consult the RMD file of the session we had on logistic regression.

In answering the questions below be succinct but provide complete answers with quantitative evidence as far as possible. Feel free to discuss methods with each other and with the tutors during the workshop. As this is an individual assignment, do not collaborate in answering the questions below or in making investment choices.

Please knit your RMD to an HTML file. Please submit your HTML file and CSV file (for Q17). The deadline is 31st October 2024 at 11:59pm. 25% of your grade will depend on the performance of your investment choices (i.e., Q17). Please note that there is a 20% penalty on your individual assignment grade if you submit an RMD file.

Enjoy the workshop!

1.1 Load the data

First we need to start by loading the data.

lc_raw <- read_csv("LendingClub Data.csv",  skip=1) %>%  
  clean_names() # use janitor::clean_names()

2.2 Clean the data

Are there any redundant columns and rows? Are all the variables in the correct format (e.g., numeric, factor, date)? Lets fix it.

The variable loan_status contains information as to whether the loan has been repaid or charged off (i.e., defaulted). Let’s create a binary factor variable for this. This variable will be the focus of this workshop.

lc_clean<- lc_raw %>%
  select(-where(~ mean(is.na(.)) > 0.9)) %>% # drop columns with more than 90% missing data
  filter(!is.na(int_rate)) %>%   #delete empty rows
  mutate(
    issue_d = mdy(issue_d),  # lubridate::mdy() to fix date format
    term = factor(term_months),     # turn 'term' into a categorical variable
    delinq_2yrs = factor(delinq_2yrs) # turn 'delinq_2yrs' into a categorical variable
  ) %>% 
  mutate(default = dplyr::recode(loan_status, 
                      "Charged Off" = "1", 
                      "Fully Paid" = "0"))%>%
    mutate(default = as.factor(default)) %>%
  dplyr::select(-emp_title,-installment, -term_months, everything()) #move some not-so-important variables to the end.

2.3 Explore the data (Q1)

Let’s explore loan defaults by creating different visualizations. We start with examining how prevalent defaults are, whether the default rate changes by loan grade or number of delinquencies, and a couple of scatter plots of defaults against loan amount and income.

#bar chart of defaults
def_vis1 <- ggplot(data=lc_clean, aes(x=default)) +
  geom_bar(aes(y = (..count..)/sum(..count..))) + 
  labs(x="Default, 1=Yes, 0=No", y="relative frequencies") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent) +
  geom_text(aes( label = scales::percent((..count..)/sum(..count..) ),y=(..count..)/sum(..count..) ), stat= "count",vjust=-0.5) 

def_vis1

#bar chart of defaults per loan grade
def_vis2 <- ggplot(data=lc_clean, aes(x=default), group=grade) +
  geom_bar(aes(y = (..count..)/sum(..count..), fill = factor(..x..)), stat="count")  + 
  labs(title="Defaults by Grade", x="Default, 1=Yes, 0=No", y="relative frequencies")+
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent) +facet_grid(~grade) + theme(legend.position = "none") +
  geom_text(aes( label = scales::percent((..count..)/sum(..count..) ),y=(..count..)/sum(..count..) ), stat= "count",vjust=-0.5) 
def_vis2

#bar chart of defaults per number of Delinquencies
def_vis3 <- lc_clean %>%
  filter(as.numeric(delinq_2yrs)<4) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=default), group=delinq_2yrs) +
  geom_bar(aes(y = (..count..)/sum(..count..), fill = factor(..x..)), stat="count")  + 
  labs(title="Defaults by Number of Delinquencies", x="Default, 1=Yes, 0=No", y="relative frequencies")  +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent) +facet_grid(~delinq_2yrs) + theme(legend.position = "none") +
  geom_text(aes( label = scales::percent((..count..)/sum(..count..) ),y=(..count..)/sum(..count..) ), stat= "count",vjust=-0.5)

def_vis3

#scatter plots 

#We select 2000 random loans to display only to make the display less busy. 
set.seed(1234)
reduced<-lc_clean[sample(0:nrow(lc_clean), 2000, replace = FALSE),]%>%
  mutate(default=as.numeric(default)-1) # also convert default to a numeric {0,1} to make it easier to plot.

          
# scatter plot of defaults against loan amount  
# If the jitter plot does not show up, try to remove I() and simply use x=loan_amnt/1000
def_vis4 <- ggplot(data=reduced, aes(y=default,x=I(loan_amnt/1000)))  + 
  labs(y="Default, 1=Yes, 0=No", x="Loan Amnt (1000 $)") +
  geom_jitter(width=0, height=0.05, alpha=0.7) #We use jitter to offset the display of defaults/non-defaults to make the data easier to interpert. We have also changed the amount to 1000$ to reduce the number of zeros on the horizontal axis.

def_vis4

#scatter plot of defaults against loan amount.
def_vis5 <- ggplot(data=reduced, aes(y=default,x=I(annual_inc/1000)))   + labs(y="Default, 1=Yes, 0=No", x="Annual Income(1000 $)") +geom_jitter(width=0, height=0.05, alpha=0.7) +  xlim(0,400)

def_vis5

Q1. Add one more visualization of your own. Describe what it shows and what you learn from it in 1-2 lines.

Insert your code here:

# My visualization
# Load the data and define interest rate groups
lc_clean %>% 
  mutate(
    # Create a new variable 'int_group' that categorizes 'int_rate' into ranges
    int_group = cut(int_rate, breaks = c(0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25), 
                    labels = c("5%-10%", "10%-15%", "15%-20%", "20%-25$%"))
  ) %>% 
  # Start ggplot with 'default' on x-axis, grouping by 'int_group'
  ggplot(aes(x = default), group = int_group) +
  
  # Create a bar plot showing the proportion of defaults within each group
  geom_bar(aes(y = (..count..) / sum(..count..), fill = factor(..x..)), stat = "count")  + 
  
  # Add labels and title for the plot
  labs(
    title = "Defaults by Interest Rate", 
    x = "Default, 1=Yes, 0=No", 
    y = "Relative Frequencies"
  )  +
  
  # Convert y-axis values to percentages for easier interpretation
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  
  # Create separate panels (facets) for each 'int_group' category
  facet_grid(~int_group) + 
  
  # Remove the legend for a cleaner look
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  
  # Display percentage labels on top of each bar
  geom_text(
    aes(label = scales::percent((..count..) / sum(..count..)), 
        y = (..count..) / sum(..count..)), 
    stat = "count",
    vjust = -0.5
  )

The above visualisation provides a bar chart on the percentage of defaults based on the interest rates where the interest rates are grouped with an interval of 5%. From the above chart, maximum people were lent loans with interest rate of 10-15% and has the highest defaults as well.

3 Linear vs. logistic regression for binary response variables (Q2)

It is certainly possible to use the OLS approach to find the line that minimizes the sum of squared errors when the dependent variable is binary (i.e., default / no default). In this case, the predicted values take the interpretation of a probability. We can also estimate a logistic regression instead. We do both below.

model_lm<-lm(as.numeric(default)~I(annual_inc/1000), lc_clean)
summary(model_lm)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = as.numeric(default) ~ I(annual_inc/1000), data = lc_clean)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -0.1595 -0.1494 -0.1444 -0.1332  1.3268 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                      Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)         1.161e+00  2.703e-03 429.312   <2e-16 ***
## I(annual_inc/1000) -2.479e-04  2.918e-05  -8.496   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.3501 on 37867 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.001903,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.001876 
## F-statistic: 72.19 on 1 and 37867 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
logistic1<-glm(default~I(annual_inc/1000), family="binomial", lc_clean)
summary(logistic1)
## 
## Call:
## glm(formula = default ~ I(annual_inc/1000), family = "binomial", 
##     data = lc_clean)
## 
## Coefficients:
##                      Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
## (Intercept)        -1.5191545  0.0292430  -51.95   <2e-16 ***
## I(annual_inc/1000) -0.0040801  0.0003998  -10.21   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)
## 
##     Null deviance: 31130  on 37868  degrees of freedom
## Residual deviance: 31005  on 37867  degrees of freedom
## AIC: 31009
## 
## Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 5
ggplot(data=reduced, aes(x=annual_inc/1000, y=default)) + 
  geom_smooth(method="lm", se=0, aes(color="OLS"))+ 
  geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family = "binomial"),  se=0, aes(color="Logistic"))+ 
  labs(y="Prob of Default", x="Annual Income(1000 $)")+  
  xlim(0,450)+scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent)+geom_jitter(width=0, height=0.05, alpha=0.7) + 
  scale_colour_manual(name="Fitted Model", values=c("blue", "red"))
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

Q2. Which model is more suitable for predicting probability of default, the linear regression or the logistic? Why?

Answer here: Logistic regression is better model because linear regression is useful for predicting values and can predict probabilities less than 0 or higher than 1 which is not correct. In the graph above, the linear model line goes below 0%. However, the logistic regression predicts the probabilities in correct range, making it easier to classify.

4 Multivariate logistic regression (Q3, Q4)

We can estimate logistic regression with multiple explanatory variables as well. Let’s use annual_inc, term, grade, and loan_amnt as features. Let’s call this model logistic2.

logistic2<- glm(default~annual_inc + term + grade + loan_amnt, family="binomial", lc_clean)
summary(logistic2)

Q3. Based on logistic 2, explain the following:
a. Explain briefly the logic of MLE (maximum likelihood estimation).
b. What does the standard error of a coefficient mean?
c. What does the p-value of a coefficient mean?
d. What does deviance mean?
e. What does AIC mean?
f. What does null deviance mean?
g. Is Logistic 2 a better model than logistic 1? Why or why not?

Answer here:
a. Likelihood determines the possibility of the predicting the correct outcome given the model parameters. Maximum likelihood estimation is a method to maximise this likelihood by adjusting the co-efficients of the model.

b. The standard error of the coefficient determines how precisely the model estimates the effect of an independent variable on the dependent variable

c. The p-value of the co-efficient tells the significance of the co-efficient (independent variable) on determining the dependent variable

d. Deviance measures the deviation of predicted results from actual data.

e. AIC is similar to deviance but it penalises for the number of co-efficients.

f. Null-Deviance means the deviation in predicted results when no co-efficients are considered but only the intercept. It acts as a base for comparing deviances.

g. Logistic 2 model is better because it allocates more variables that reduces the deviance from 31130 to 29286.

4.1 From probability to classification (Q5-Q10)

The logistic regression model gives us a sense of how likely defaults are; it gives us a probability estimate. To convert this into a prediction, we need to choose a cutoff probability and classify every loan with a predicted probability of default above the cutoff as a prediction of default (and vice versa for loans with a predicted probability below this cutoff).

Let’s choose a threshold of 16%. Of course some of our predictions will turn out to be right but some will turn out to be wrong – you can see this in the density figures of the previous section. Let’s call “default” the “positive” class since this is the class we are trying to predict. We could be making two types of mistakes. False positives (i.e., predict that a loan will default when it will not) and false negatives (i.e., predict that a loan will not default when it does). These errors are summarized in the confusion matrix.

Q6. Using the confusion matrix, explain the following and show how they are calculated a.1. Accuracy a.2. Sensitivity a.3. Specificity For each of this explain what they mean in the context of the lending club and the goal of predicting loan defaults.

Answer here:

a.1. Accuracy = Total correct predictions / Total predictions = (TP+TN)/(TP+TN+FP+FN)

a.2. Sensitivity = True Positives / (True Positives + False Negatives) = TP/(TP+FN)

a.3. Specificity = True Negatives / (True Negatives + False Positives) = TN/(TN+FP)

Q8. Previously, we compared the performance of the logistic2 model with different cutoff values (16% and 20%). Explain what the ROC shows and what the AUC measure means. Why do we expect the AUC of any predictive model to be between 0.5 and 1? Could the AUC ever be below 0.5 or above 1?

Insert your code here:

# Calculate the ROC curve for 'logistic2' model
# 'roc' function takes the actual default outcomes and predicted probabilities of default (prob_default2)

## Setting levels: control = 0, case = 1
## Setting direction: controls < cases

# Extract the AUC from the ROC object and store it in 'AUC2'
AUC2 <- ROC_logistic2$auc

# Plot the ROC curve with the ggroc function and display the AUC in the plot title
ggroc(ROC_logistic2, alpha = 0.5) + 
  
  # Add a title to the plot, embedding the AUC value rounded to two decimal places
  ggtitle(paste("Model Logistic 2: AUC =", round(AUC2 * 100, digits = 2), "%"))  +
  
  # Add a dashed diagonal line representing a random classifier (where TPR = FPR)
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1, xend = 0, y = 0, yend = 1), color = "grey", linetype = "dashed") +
  
  # Add dashed segments for the x and y-axis extremes (TPR = 1 and FPR = 1) for clearer reference
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1, xend = 1, y = 0, yend = 1), color = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1, xend = 0, y = 1, yend = 1), color = "black", linetype = "dashed")

Provide comments here:

i. ROC: It plots the Sensitivity against Specificity for different thresholds.

ii. AUC: It indicates the area under the ROC curve which quantifies the overall performance of the model.

iii. If the AUC is 0.5, the model is clearly performing random guessing. Any record has an equal probability to be Yes or No similar to coin toss. As the AUC approaches to 1, the classifier is performing better. AUC = 1 indicates the perfect model for classification.

iv. If the AUC is less than 0.5, the model is worse than a random guessing model.

4.2 Selecting loans to invest in using the model Logistic 2. (Q11)

Before we look for a better model than logistic 2 let’s see how we can use this model to select loans to invest. Let’s make the simplistic assumption that every loan generates $15 profit if it is paid off and $75 loss if it is charged off for an investor. Let’s use a cut-off value to determine which loans to invest in, that is, if the predicted probability of default for a loan is below this value then we invest in that loan and not if it is above.

To do this we split the data in three parts: training, validation, and testing. Feel free to experiment with different seeds but please use the seeds provided below for your submission.

# splitting the data into training and testing
set.seed(24)
train_test_split <- initial_split(lc_clean, prop = 0.6)
training <- training(train_test_split) #60% of the data is set aside for training
remaining <- testing(train_test_split) #40% of the data is set aside for validation & testing
set.seed(2024)
train_test_split <- initial_split(remaining, prop = 0.5)
validation<-training(train_test_split) #50% of the remaining data (20% of total data) will be used for validation
testing<-testing(train_test_split) #50% of the remaining data (20% of total data) will be used for testing

Q11. Train logistic 2 on the training set above. Use the trained model to determine the optimal cut-off threshold based on the validation test. What is the optimal cutoff threshold? How much profit does it generate? Using the testing set, what is the profit per loan associated with the cutoff?

Insert your code here:

#estimate the model on the training set
# Train a logistic regression model (logistic2) to predict 'default' using specified predictors
logistic2 <- glm(default ~ annual_inc + term + grade + loan_amnt, family = "binomial", data = training)
## Warning: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred
# Make predictions on the validation set using the logistic2 model
# 'type = "response"' returns predicted probabilities of default
p_val <- predict(logistic2, validation, type = "response")

# Define profit and loss per classification outcome
unit_profit <- 15   # profit per correctly predicted non-default (TN)
unit_loss <- 75     # loss per incorrectly predicted default (FP)

# Initialize vectors to store profit and threshold values
profit <- 0           # profit at each threshold
threshold <- 0        # threshold values (from 0.0025 to 0.25, incremented by 0.0025)

# Loop over 100 threshold values from 0.0025 to 0.25 in steps of 0.0025
for(i in 1:100) {
  # Calculate the current threshold value
  threshold[i] <- i / 400
  
  # Classify predictions as 1 (default) or 0 (non-default) based on the current threshold
  classify_one_or_zero <- ifelse(p_val > threshold[i], 1, 0)
  
  # Generate a confusion matrix to evaluate predictions against actual outcomes
  cm <- confusionMatrix(as.factor(classify_one_or_zero), as.factor(validation$default), positive = "1")
  
  # Calculate profit: true negatives (cm$table[1,1]) yield profit; false positives (cm$table[1,2]) incur loss
  profit[i] <- cm$table[1, 1] * unit_profit - cm$table[1, 2] * unit_loss
}

# Plot the profit curve over different threshold values
ggplot(as.data.frame(threshold), aes(x = threshold, y = profit)) +
  geom_smooth(method = 'loess', se = 0) +
  labs(title = "Profit curve with random classifier")
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

# Find the maximum profit and corresponding threshold
profit_max <- max(profit)
threshold_max <- threshold[which.max(profit)] * 100

# Print the maximum profit and the optimal threshold as percentages
print(profit_max)
## [1] 31050
print(threshold_max)
## [1] 16.5
# Generate predicted probabilities of default for the testing set using the logistic2 model
p_test <- predict(logistic2, testing, type = "response")

# Classify predictions as 1 (default) or 0 (non-default) based on a threshold of 16.5%
classify_one_or_zero_test <- ifelse(p_test > 0.165, 1, 0)

# Create a confusion matrix comparing predictions with actual default values in the testing set
cm_test <- confusionMatrix(as.factor(classify_one_or_zero_test), as.factor(testing$default), positive = "1")

# Calculate profit on the testing set:
# Profit = (True Negatives * unit profit) - (False Positives * unit loss)
profit_test <- cm_test$table[1, 1] * unit_profit - cm_test$table[1, 2] * unit_loss

# Print the profit obtained on the testing set
print(profit_test)
## [1] 33225

Insert your comments here: The threshold probability that generates maximum profit is 16.5 the corresponding profit generated is 31050. The profit for test set is 16500.

5 More realistic revenue model (Q12-Q18)

Let’s build a more realistic profit and loss model. Each loan has different terms (e.g., different interest rate and different duration) and therefore a different return if fully paid. For example, a 36 month loan of $5000 with instalment of $163 per month would generate a return of 163*36/5000-1=17.36% if there was no default. Let’s assume that it would generate a loss of -60% if there was a default (the loss is not 100% because the loan may not default immediately and/or the lending club may be able to recover part of the loan).

Q12. Under these assumptions, how much return would you get if you invested $1 in each loan in the validation set? Express your answer as a % return.

Insert your code here:

#add code here
# Classify observations in the validation set as 1 (default) or 0 (non-default) using a 16.5% threshold
classify_mt <- ifelse(p_val > 0.165, 1, 0)

# Initialize counters for missed non-defaults and total return on investment (ROI)
misses <- 0    # Count of defaults that were incorrectly classified as non-defaults
ROI <- 0       # Total ROI based on classifications
counter <- 1   # Initialize a counter for row indexing in the loop

# Loop through each classification result in 'classify_mt'
for (i in classify_mt) {
  
  # Check if the classification is 0 (non-default) and the actual outcome in the validation set is also 0
  if (i == 0 & validation[counter,]$default == 0) {
    
    # If correct non-default prediction, calculate return based on loan terms
    # ROI is increased by ((term * installment amount / loan amount) - 1), which represents loan return
    ROI <- ROI + ((((validation[counter,]$term_months * validation[counter,]$installment) / validation[counter,]$loan_amnt) - 1))
  
  # Check if classification is 0 (non-default) but actual outcome is 1 (default)
  } else if (i == 0 & validation[counter,]$default == 1) {
    
    # If incorrect non-default prediction, apply a fixed loss of 60% of the loan amount
    ROI <- ROI - 0.6
    
    # Increase the 'misses' counter to record the misclassification
    misses <- misses + 1
  }
  
  # Move to the next row in the validation set
  counter <- counter + 1
}

# Calculate the average ROI as a percentage
avg_ROI <- (ROI / nrow(validation)) * 100

# Print the average ROI as a percentage
print(avg_ROI)
## [1] 6.586861

Insert comments here: The average return after investing $1 on all investments is 11.11%

Q13. Take the exact same setting as in Q10; however, assume that each time there is default we further incur a fixed cost of $ \(C\) in addition to the 60% loss. What is the maximum amount of \(C\) which would still give a positive mean return in the previous setting (i.e., investing $ 1 in each loan).

Insert your code here:

#add code here
# Define a function 'avg_return' that calculates the average return on investment (ROI)
# given a specific cost added to the default scenario
avg_return <- function(cost) {
  
  # For each loan in the validation set, calculate 'loan_return' based on whether there was a default
  # - If no default (default == "0"), return = (installment * term months / loan amount) - 1, indicating profit
  # - If default (default == "1"), return = -0.6 - cost, where -0.6 is the standard loss and 'cost' is an additional fixed cost
  validation <- validation %>%
    mutate(loan_return = ifelse(default == "0", installment * term_months / loan_amnt - 1, -0.6 - cost))
  
  # Calculate the average ROI (avg_ROI) across all loans in the validation set
  avg_ROI <- mean(validation$loan_return)
  
  # Return the average ROI value
  return(avg_ROI)
}

# Define a range of cost values from 0 to 1 in increments of 0.01 to evaluate
cost_range <- seq(0, 1, 0.01)

# Apply the 'avg_return' function across each cost in 'cost_range' using 'sapply'
# - This produces a vector 'avg_returns_values' of average ROI values for each cost in the range
avg_returns_values <- sapply(cost_range, avg_return)

# Identify the maximum cost for which the average ROI is still positive
max_cost <- max(cost_range[avg_returns_values > 0])

# Print the maximum allowable cost that maintains a positive average ROI
print(max_cost)
## [1] 0.74

Insert comments here: A fixed cost of $0.74 for every missed prediction of default would still return a positive mean ROI. Further fixed cost, would result a negative ROI.

From here onward, drop the assumption of an additional fixed cost as introduced in Q11 and take the revenue model introduced in Q10. Unfortunately, we cannot use the realized return to select loans to invest (as at the time we make the investment decision we do not know which loan will default). Instead, we can calculate an expected return using the estimated probabilities of default – expected return = return if not default * (1-prob(default)) + return if default * prob(default).

y_train <- training$def_chr

# Fit LASSO model with cross-validation to select optimal lambda
lasso_model <- cv.glmnet(X_train, y_train, alpha = 1, family = "binomial")

# Extract the best lambda value based on minimum cross-validation error
min_lambda <- lasso_model$lambda.min

# Fit the LASSO model with the optimal lambda
model_lasso <- glmnet(X_train, y_train, family = "binomial", alpha = 1, lambda = min_lambda)

# Predict on the training set and calculate training AUC
train_pred <- predict(model_lasso, newx = X_train, type = "response")
train_roc <- roc(y_train, as.vector(train_pred))
## Setting levels: control = D, case = P
## Setting direction: controls < cases
train_auc <- auc(train_roc)

# Prepare testing data and calculate AUC for validation
X_val <- model.matrix(formula, data = testing)[, -1]
y_val <- as.numeric(as.character(testing$def_chr))
## Warning: NAs introduced by coercion
# Predict on the validation set and calculate validation AUC
val_pred <- predict(model_lasso, newx = X_val, type = "response")
val_roc <- roc(y_train, as.vector(train_pred))
## Setting levels: control = D, case = P
## Setting direction: controls < cases
val_auc <- auc(val_roc)

# Display AUC for training and testing sets
cat("AUC for LASSO model testing set:", val_auc, "\n")
## AUC for LASSO model testing set: 0.6864864
cat("AUC for LASSO model training set:", train_auc, "\n")
## AUC for LASSO model training set: 0.6864864

Q17. The file “Assessment Data_2024.csv” contains information on almost \(1,800\) new loans. Use your best model (see previous question) to choose 240 loans to invest in. For this question assume that the loss proportion is 60%. Your grade on this question will be based on the actual performance of your choices.

# Read the assessment data CSV file and create new features
lc_assessment <- read_csv("D:\\data_science_business\\assignment2\\Assessment Data_2024.csv") %>%
  mutate(
    term = as.factor(`term (months)`),                       # Convert 'term' to factor
    grade = as.factor(grade),                                # Convert 'grade' to factor
    home_ownership = factor(home_ownership),                 # Convert 'home_ownership' to factor
    emp_length = factor(emp_length),                         # Convert 'emp_length' to factor
    income_loan_ratio = annual_inc / loan_amnt,              # Calculate income-to-loan ratio
    log_inc = log(annual_inc + 1),                           # Apply log transformation to income
    term_grade_intr = as.numeric(term) * as.numeric(grade),  # Interaction term: 'term' * 'grade'
    inc_grade_intr = annual_inc * as.numeric(grade)          # Interaction term: income * 'grade'
  )
## Rows: 1799 Columns: 14
## ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## Delimiter: ","
## chr (5): grade, emp_length, home_ownership, verification_status, issue_d
## dbl (7): Loan number, int_rate, loan_amnt, term (months), dti, delinq_2yrs, ...
## num (1): installment
## lgl (1): emp_title
## 
## ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
## ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
# Align factor levels in assessment data with training data for consistency
lc_assessment$term <- factor(lc_assessment$term, levels = levels(training$term))
lc_assessment$grade <- factor(lc_assessment$grade, levels = levels(training$grade))
lc_assessment$home_ownership <- factor(lc_assessment$home_ownership, levels = levels(training$home_ownership))
lc_assessment$emp_length <- factor(lc_assessment$emp_length, levels = levels(training$emp_length))

# Define the model formula for prediction without the response variable
predict_formula <- ~ annual_inc + loan_amnt + income_loan_ratio + log_inc + term + grade + emp_length + inc_grade_intr + term_grade_intr

# Create a model matrix for assessment data to match the structure of training data
X_asmnt <- model.matrix(predict_formula, data = lc_assessment)[, -1]

# Identify missing columns in X_assessment and add them as zero columns for consistency
missing_cols <- setdiff(colnames(X_train), colnames(X_asmnt))
if (length(missing_cols) > 0) {
  X_asmnt <- cbind(X_asmnt, Matrix(0, nrow = nrow(X_asmnt), ncol = length(missing_cols)))
  colnames(X_asmnt)[(ncol(X_asmnt) - length(missing_cols) + 1):ncol(X_asmnt)] <- missing_cols
}

# Ensure column order in X_assessment matches that in X_train
X_asmnt <- X_asmnt[, colnames(X_train)]

# Predict default probabilities using the trained LASSO model
predict_probs <- predict(model_lasso, newx = X_asmnt, type = "response")

# Calculate expected returns for each loan in the assessment data
lc_assessment <- lc_assessment %>%
  mutate(
    predicted_prob = as.vector(predict_probs),               # Store predicted probabilities
    installment = as.numeric(installment),                   # Convert 'installment' to numeric
    term_months = as.numeric(`term (months)`),               # Convert 'term' to numeric
    loan_amnt = as.numeric(loan_amnt),                       # Convert 'loan_amnt' to numeric
    return_if_paid = (installment * term_months) / loan_amnt - 1, # Expected return if loan is paid in full
    return_if_default = -0.6,                                # Expected return if loan defaults
    expected_return = return_if_paid * (1 - predict_probs) + return_if_default * predict_probs # Calculate expected return
  )

# Select the top 240 loans based on expected return
selected_loans <- lc_assessment %>%
  arrange(desc(expected_return)) %>%                         # Sort loans by expected return
  slice_head(n = 240) %>%                                    # Select top 240 loans
  mutate(roopa_yashaswini = 1) %>%                           # Label selected loans with 1
  select(`Loan number`, roopa_yashaswini)

# Label remaining (non-selected) loans with 0
non_selected_loans <- lc_assessment %>%
  filter(!`Loan number` %in% selected_loans$`Loan number`) %>% # Filter non-selected loans
  mutate(roopa_yashaswini = 0) %>%                           # Label non-selected loans with 0
  select(`Loan number`, roopa_yashaswini)

# Combine selected and non-selected loans, keeping original order
final_selection <- bind_rows(selected_loans, non_selected_loans) %>%
  arrange(`Loan number`) %>%                                 # Arrange by loan number
  rename(loan_number = `Loan number`)                        # Rename column for output

# Save the final selection to a CSV file
write.csv(final_selection, "Roopa_Yashaswini.csv", row.names = FALSE)

Q18. (Optional)

At a high level, what we have done in this assignment is a two-step process: (1) building a prediction model for loan defaults and (2) making decisions on which loans to invest in.

When we build our prediction model, our goal is to make accurate predictions on testing data (accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, AUC, AIC, etc.). When we make our investment decisions, our goal is to maximize profit (in our case, the average return of the selected loans in the testing data). Do you think a good prediction model always leads to a good investment decision? If this is not always the case, why or why not?

Some loans offer higher returns than others. Are they equally important when we make our investment decisions? One argument is that we should care more about our prediction performance on high-return loans because we want to invest in non-defaulting, high-return loans. Try to modify your prediction model based on this idea, explain your model, and interpret its performance.
